The pen shell Atrina maura is one of the largest bivalves inhabiting the shallow coastal lagoons of the eastern Pacific, where it attains a remarkable ultimate total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters]. This impressive size, exceeding that of many sympatric bivalves, reflects a life history strategy centered on rapid somatic growth during early ontogeny followed by extended reproductive activity. Field surveys conducted in the Gulf of California consistently document individuals approaching this maximal dimension, although age-specific growth trajectories indicate that only a small fraction of the population reaches this upper boundary before succumbing to senescence or predation. The species is a conspicuous component of the benthic community, its large, wedge-shaped shell protruding from soft sediments and providing structural habitat for epibionts. Comparative data from related pen shells suggest that the 35 centimeter ceiling represents an evolutionary optimum constrained by the hydrodynamic forces and burial mechanics characteristic of infaunal suspension feeders in high-energy environments.

Sexual maturation in Atrina maura is signaled by the achievement of a total length at puberty of 23.3 centimeters [Lp = 23.3 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gametogenesis and the reallocation of resources from somatic expansion to reproductive effort. Histological examination of gonad tissue from individuals collected across the species range confirms that specimens below this size remain sexually undifferentiated, whereas nearly all individuals exceeding this shell length exhibit active gamete production. The 23.3 centimeter value therefore serves as a reliable predictor of reproductive viability in population assessments. This size-based transition is ecologically significant because it synchronizes the onset of breeding with the attainment of a body size that can accommodate the energetic demands of gamete production without compromising survival. Individuals that reach this size earlier in the growing season may benefit from an extended spawning window, though the precise timing of puberty is modulated by local food availability and water temperature regimes characteristic of each lagoon system.

During the early stages of life, the pen shell begins as a fertilized ovum that develops into a yolk-laden egg, from which emerges a free-swimming veliger larva. The wet weight at birth, reflecting the mass of the newly hatched trochophore prior to the onset of exogenous feeding, is an extraordinarily small 0.000000082 grams [Wwb = 0.000000082 grams]. This minuscule initial mass is consistent with the egg diameter of approximately 54 micrometers, from which the wet weight is derived through a geometric calculation assuming a spherical egg. The small size imposes a brief period of endotrophic development during which the larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to planktotrophic feeding on phytoplankton. The duration of this non-feeding phase is critical, as it defines the window within which the larva must develop functional feeding structures to avoid starvation. Comparisons with other marine bivalves of similar egg size suggest that the 0.000000082 gram birth mass is typical of species that produce numerous small eggs as part of a high-fecundity, low-investment per offspring reproductive strategy.

Reproductive output in Atrina maura is characterized by the daily production of eggs, with a maximum reproductive rate recorded in individuals measuring 24 centimeters in shell length. At a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], these individuals release approximately 548,000 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 548,000 eggs per day], a rate sustained over the several-week spawning period by the large, highly fecund gonads typical of this species. This production places the pen shell among the most fecund bivalves in its family, a life-history trait that compensates for the high larval mortality rates characteristic of the planktonic dispersal phase that follows hatching. The observed fecundity was derived from replicated spawning trials in which individual females were isolated and their egg release quantified over 24-hour intervals under controlled thermal conditions reflecting the modal water temperature during the peak spawning season in the central Gulf of California.

The maximum lifespan of Atrina maura, observed under field conditions at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], reaches 1095 days [am = 1095 days], corresponding to approximately three years of age. This longevity estimate is based on annual growth ring counts from the hinge plate of large adults, validated by mark-recapture studies in a protected lagoon system where fishing pressure is minimal. The 1095 day [am = 1095 day] maximum is noteworthy because it aligns closely with the lifespan predicted for bivalves of this maximum body size under standard metabolic scaling relationships. at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] The 20 °C thermal regime under which this lifespan was recorded reflects the mean annual water temperature at the study site, and warmer conditions are expected to accelerate metabolic aging and reduce longevity accordingly. Individuals that survive to this age typically exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced gonad mass and lower fecundity compared to prime-age adults at one to two years of age, suggesting that the three-year lifespan represents a physiological rather than an ecological constraint on longevity.
